note: What this file is (plain words): the structured result of the wet street painter test (20 October 2026), the same content that was returned to the workflow. The full plain-language report is "notes - wet street painter test.md".
summary: ONE repaint of the wet lockout plate with a brief changed to keep the wet look. The wet look mostly survived: darker glossy road, lamp/window/brazier reflections in the same places (overlap of bright areas 0.63 against 0.04 for the dry painting), gutter puddles with mirrored houses, sett highlights; the blown-out glare pool was tamed. Faults: pale white brush-stroke clouds added to the sky, far lamp streaks made much stronger, walls do not read wet, brightest road bit still 1.21 times the notice. Lined up with the plate with almost no correction (stretch 0.9995, shift -0.5/+0.5 px). In the film stage the wet look holds in the plate view and the moved view, BUT the film dry behind painting shows on 71 % of the road pixels of the moved view (dry ghosts next to the wet road), and the stage curve darkens the wet painting (road 0.75 of painted against 0.92 for dry). Cost US$0.197 to 0.277 (not 10 cents: price is 4.8 cents a megapixel), 1 call, under the US$0.30 limit.

prompt: Repaint image 1 completely as a hand-painted illustration in the exact painting style of image 2: the same visible brush strokes, dark ink outlines, simplified painterly textures on brick, stone, slate and wood, and painted wet shine and painted reflections. Nothing should look like a 3D render or a photograph any more. It is a pit-village street at dusk on 1 May 1926, wet after rain. Keep image 1's camera, framing, perspective and every shape, outline, size and position exactly as they are, and keep its pattern of light and dark; change only the brushwork and the colour handling. Keep: the rusty drum with its open top, dull dark rust-brown, not orange, its top a dark sooty hollow with only a faint orange glow low inside behind the front rim; the dark timber notice board on its two posts with the cream notice (plain paper with grey rows of print-like marks, no readable letters); the small wooden pail at the foot of the board, with no handle; the black gas lamps on their posts down both sides of the street; the brick terraces and stone cottages, the colliery building, its tall chimney and winding wheels; the wooden handcart on the left with its big spoked wheel and the spade leaning on it; the pile of coal sacks in the road; the small heap of black coal lumps on the road; the dustbin at the right edge; and the ladder on the left pavement. The colliery gates are shut: thin dark iron bars across a dim grey doorway whose big doors are closed. Every gas lamp has warm amber glass with a small bright gas mantle inside. The gutter beside the kerb is a shallow, smooth stone channel with no steps, ridges or grating, with the rainwater lying in it as image 1 shows. The road, pavement and walls are cool blue-grey dusk, and the brick is weathered and greyed by coal smoke without getting any darker. The street is wet after rain, and image 1 shows exactly where. Keep all of that wet look exactly where image 1 has it, at the same size and the same strength, painted in the hand of image 2 (painted reflections made of flat shapes of colour with a few ink lines and visible brush strokes; not a photograph, not a mirror): the wet sheen on the setts of the road and on the pavement flags; the lamp, lit-window and brazier reflections lying on the road as soft painted streaks and pools of warm light; the soft reflections of the handcart and the sacks on the road under them; the puddles in the gutters and in the low spots of the road, each one a smooth painted sheet of cool grey-blue with the houses, lamps and lit windows mirrored upside down in it; the thin dark wet lines between the setts and between the flags; and the darker, damper foot of the walls. The road is darker and glossier than a dry road, and never looks dry. Add no wet look where image 1 has none. Warm light stays only where it already is: round the drum, on the board, at the lamps, in the few lit windows, and in their reflections on the wet road where image 1 shows them. Nothing is brighter than the notice. Thin parts (the lamp arms, the gate bars, the cart's rails and spokes, the spade's handle, the winding rope) stay thin and exactly in place, or are left out; never thicken them. Where two things meet or nearly meet, keep each edge exactly where it is and never join them: the drum's side and the board's left post, each gas-lamp head and the wall pipe and bracket beside it, the far lamps and the house downpipes, the spade and the cart's wheel; the winding rope never joins the lamp. Never add: flames, sparks, smoke or steam anywhere (not from the drum, not from any chimney); glows, halos or light rays round any light, the notice or the drum (the wet road's reflections of the lights are not halos: keep those as image 1 has them); a handle on the pail; people, animals or birds; extra props (no coal tub, rails, barrel, crates or litter in the road or on the pavement); a moon, stars or bright clouds; new signs or lettering; new or longer shadows.

PROBLEM: the stage shows the film DRY behind painting round the near props once the camera moves: about 18 % of the moved frame, 71 % of its road pixels and 70 % of its pavement pixels, giving a pale dry ghost beside the drum and dry pavement at the foot; wet painting used as its own behind painting removes it (stand-in only). Rough share of moved frame: painting 75 %, behind painting 18 %, own 3D surface 7 %. recommendation: As proof: yes, the painter keeps the wet look when the brief asks for it. As the picture for the lockout clip: not yet. Needed, with cost: (1) sky: brief wording for dark soft clouds (one more repaint about US$0.20-0.28 with small pictures, up to 0.43 at full size if inputs are charged, painter already ignored no bright clouds once) OR composite the old dry sky into the wet painting (free, under an hour, untested); (2) a WET behind painting with the props painted out (one more repaint about US$0.20-0.26 with a small picture sent) before any camera move, otherwise dry ghosts on 71 % of the moved road; (3) lift dark values of the wet painting or the stage curve for wet scenes (free, 2-3 minutes a test, untested) because the stage darkens it to 0.75; (4) plate (Blender, free, 20-50 minutes): lower the road Film Coat/Specular Boost so the glare pool is not brighter than the notice, give the walls a visible wet foot and props wet contact; needs another repaint to show. Only one painting exists, so repeatability is unknown. Real price per 2k repaint is about US$0.20-0.28, not 10 cents.
